draft.title: Judging a liveability strategy
card: A strategy is a plan to improve a place. To judge it, first set criteria, which are the tests you will use.
Common criteria are cost, who benefits and the effect on the environment.
Then weigh the strategy against each criterion. A plan may do well on one and poorly on another.
Last, reach a decision and give reasons that use the criteria.
draft.remember: Set criteria first, then weigh the strategy against each one before deciding.

a.q: A council plans a new skate park. Which question uses the criterion of who benefits?
opts: Which groups in the community would use it?
How much will the concrete cost?
Will it use up any bushland?
How long will the building work take?
a.why: Who benefits asks which people would gain from the strategy. The cost question is about money, and the bushland question is about the environment.
a.clue: Look for the question about people.

b.q: A council in Western Australia plans a new bus route. It is cheap and used by many people, but it needs bushland to be cleared. What is the best way to judge it?
opts: Weigh it against cost, who benefits and environmental effect
Approve it because it is cheap
Reject it because it clears bushland
Approve it because many people would use it
b.why: A fair judgement weighs the plan against every criterion. Looking at only one, such as cost or the bushland, ignores the others.
b.clue: Judge against all the criteria, not only one.

a.best: Which groups in the community would use it?

b.best: Weigh it against cost, who benefits and environmental effect

problems.detail: The right option is the only one that names all three criteria in the card's own words. It is also the only one that describes a method rather than a quick approve or reject decision, and it is slightly the longest. A student could pick it by matching the card's wording without understanding how to weigh a strategy.

check.summary: The facts and the intended answers are correct. In question b the right option stands out: it repeats the card's list of criteria and is the only option that is a method rather than a decision, so consider rewording the options so each one describes a way of judging.

How long will the building work take?

b.q: A council in Western Australia plans a new bus route. It is cheap and well used, but bushland must be cleared. Whose thinking follows the steps for judging it?
opts: Ava: cheap and well used, but the lost bushland counts too
Ben: cheap and well used, so the council should go ahead
Cal: bushland would be cleared, so the plan should stop
Dee: well used, so the cost and bushland do not matter
b.why: Ava weighs the plan against all three criteria: cost, who benefits and the environment. Ben is tempting because he uses two criteria, but he leaves out the effect on the environment. Cal and Dee each look at only one.
b.clue: Who checks the plan against every criterion?
